rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The prohibition may address the victim’s guardian: he must not kill anyone under this ruling excessively.
rows.anchor: ويصح أن يراد به الولي أي فلا تسرف أيها الولي في قتل أحد

rows.speaker: أبو مسلم السراج
rows.claim: He read the verb in the third person as an indicative statement, a reading that fits only the guardian interpretation.
rows.anchor: وقرأ أبو مسلم السراج صاحب الدعوة العباسية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn Atiyya questions relying on Abu Muslim as an authority for a Qur’anic reading.
rows.anchor: وفي الاحتجاج بأبي مسلم في القراءة نظر

rows.speaker: أبي بن كعب
rows.claim: Ubayy’s reading addresses guardians in the plural and explicitly says the slain person’s guardian is supported.
rows.anchor: فلا تسرفوا في القتل إن ولي المقتول كان منصورا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Among readings of the pronoun in “he is supported,” Ibn Atiyya prefers the murdered victim, since he is the wronged party and support is associated with the wronged.
rows.anchor: والضمير في قوله إنه عائد على الولي، وقيل على المقتول، وهو عندي أرجح الأقوال

rows.speaker: أبو عبيد
rows.claim: Abu Ubayd takes the pronoun to refer to the killer, who is supposedly delivered from the afterlife’s punishment by being killed; Ibn Atiyya calls this remote and weak.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو عبيد على القاتل لأنه إذا قتل في الدنيا وخلص بذلك من عذاب الآخرة

rows.speaker: الضحاك
rows.claim: Al-Dahhak says this was the first Qur’anic revelation concerning killing, and that it is Meccan.
rows.anchor: وقال الضحاك هذه أول ما نزل من القرآن في شأن القتل وهي مكية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The address chiefly concerns guardians entrusted with orphans’ property, and also anyone who becomes involved in an orphan’s affairs without being a guardian.
rows.anchor: الخطاب في هذه الآية للأوصياء

rows.speaker: ابن السكيت
rows.claim: Ibn al-Sikkit says a human is an orphan through loss of the father, while an animal is an orphan through loss of its mother.
rows.anchor: اليتم في البشر من قبل الأب

rows.speaker: الماوردي
rows.claim: Al-Mawardi’s book also reports that human orphanhood can be caused by loss of the mother.
rows.anchor: أن اليتم في البشر من قبل الأم أيضا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The word orphan denotes a child’s being alone; the verse permits approaching the property only in the best manner or condition.
rows.anchor: إلا بالتي هي أحسن يريد إلا بأحسن الحالات

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The plural forms are aytām and yatāmā; the latter is likened to forms for burdensome conditions that overtake someone.
rows.anchor: وجمعه أيتام كشريف وأشراف وشهيد وأشهاد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A report says there is no orphanhood after puberty.
rows.anchor: وفي الحديث «لا يتم بعد حلم»

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A wealthy guardian should grow and protect the property without personally benefiting from it; this is the scrupulous and preferable course.
rows.anchor: أن يثمر المال ويحوطه ولا يمس منه شيئا على جهة الانتفاع به

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A wealthy guardian who works on the orphan’s property and is scrupulous may have a wage assigned by legal judgment.
rows.anchor: يشتغل في مال اليتيم ويشح فله بالفقه أن تفرض له أجرة

rows.speaker: عمر بن الخطاب
rows.claim: Umar says a poor guardian may borrow from the orphan’s funds and repay when financially able.
rows.anchor: عمر بن الخطاب رضي الله عنه: يتسلف منه، فإذا أيسر رد فيه

rows.speaker: ابن المسيب
rows.claim: Ibn al-Musayyib forbids even drinking water bought with the orphan’s property; he explains the allowance as compensation for service such as washing the child’s clothes.
rows.anchor: ابن المسيب، لا يشرب الماء من مال اليتيم

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujahid allows a poor guardian to engage in trade for the orphan but not to borrow from the property; he construes the allowance as drawing on one’s own funds.
rows.anchor: مجاهد: لا يقرب إلا التجارة ولا يستقرض منه

rows.speaker: أبو يوسف
rows.claim: Abu Yusuf suggests the allowance to eat by what is recognized as fair may have been abrogated by the prohibition on consuming wealth wrongfully.
rows.anchor: أبو يوسف: لعل قوله فليأكل بالمعروف

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas allows a poor guardian modest food from the estate for necessary work, provided he does not harm the child’s offspring or overmilk its livestock.
rows.anchor: ابن عباس: يأكل منه الشربة من اللبن والطرفة من الفاكهة

rows.speaker: زيد بن أسلم
rows.claim: Zayd ibn Aslam says the guardian may take only a fingertip’s worth as a livelihood in return for his labor.
rows.anchor: زيد بن أسلم: يأكل منه بأطراف أصابعه بلغة من العيش بتعبه

rows.speaker: مالك
rows.claim: Malik and others permit taking a wage proportionate to the guardian’s effort; Ibn Atiyya groups all these allowances under acting in the best manner.
rows.anchor: مالك رحمه الله وغيره: يأخذ منه أجرة بقدر تعبه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn Atiyya calls this an expression of taking little.
rows.anchor: قال القاضي أبو محمد: وهذه استعارة للتقلل

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatadah reports that the rule distressed the Muslims, who avoided eating together with orphans, after which 2:220 permitted mixing while distinguishing reformers from corrupters.
rows.anchor: عن قتادة أن هذه الآية لما نزلت شقت على المسلمين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Reaching the orphan’s maturity ends the restraint on handling the property; what follows that limit remains suspended until legal evidence or an applicable consensus establishes a rule.
rows.anchor: حتى يبلغ أشده غاية الإمساك عن مال اليتيم

rows.speaker: عائشة
rows.claim: Aisha relates that she made the Prophet’s sacrificial garlands and sent them while he continued doing what God had permitted until the sacrifice was slaughtered, illustrating the rule about limits.
rows.anchor: عائشة رضي الله عنها أنا فتلت قلائد هدي رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم بيدي

rows.speaker: سيبويه
rows.claim: Sibawayh treats ashudd as a plural of shadd.
rows.anchor: «الأشد» جمع شد عند سيبويه

rows.speaker: أبو عبيدة
rows.claim: Abu Ubayda says ashudd has no singular from the same word-form and refers to strength in judgment, experience, and self-management, which comes only with puberty.
rows.anchor: أبو عبيدة: لا واحد له من لفظه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In Malik’s school, maturity entails both puberty and financial soundness; whether religious uprightness is required is disputed among his followers.
rows.anchor: البلوغ بالاحتلام أو ما يقوم مقامه

rows.speaker: ابن القاسم
rows.claim: Ibn al-Qasim does not require religious uprightness if the person manages his property reliably; some other Maliki authorities do.
rows.anchor: فابن القاسم لا يراعيه إذا كان ضابطا لماله

rows.speaker: أبو حنيفة
rows.claim: Abu Hanifa defines maturity as puberty alone and permits no guardianship over a pubescent person unless that person is known to be profligate.
rows.anchor: ومذهب أبي حنيفة أن الأشد هو البلوغ فقط

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn Atiyya says he is not confident about the restriction in Abu Hanifa’s position as phrased here.
rows.anchor: ولست من هذا التقييد في قوله على ثقة

rows.speaker: أبو إسحاق الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjaj says ashudd begins at eighteen, but Ibn Atiyya understands this as one proposed threshold for puberty in a person who has not had a wet dream, not a requirement to withhold property from a pubescent, sound-minded person.
rows.anchor: أبو إسحاق الزجاج «الأشد» في قوله أن تأتي على الصبي ثمان عشرة سنة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The command to honor a covenant covers every binding pact with God or with people in obedience; the covenant will be asked of the person entrusted with it.
rows.anchor: وقوله بالعهد لفظ عام لكل عهد وعقد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The command is directed to traders and those measuring or weighing: they must deliver what is due in measure and weight.
rows.anchor: أمر الله تعالى في هذه الآية أهل التجر والكيل والوزن أن يعطوا الحق في كيلهم ووزنهم

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas used to warn in the market that two instruments—the measure and scale—had caused the ruin of earlier peoples.
rows.anchor: كان يقف في السوق ويقول

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The wording places the duty of completing the measure on the seller, since the buyer is not addressed as the one who fulfills it.
rows.anchor: وتقتضي هذه الآية أن الكيل على البائع

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Hasan explains qistas as the qabbān, a type of weighing scale.
rows.anchor: «القسطاس» قال الحسن هو القبان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other explanations identify qistas as a balance in general; Mujahid instead says it means justice and is a Roman word.
rows.anchor: وكان يقول هي لغة رومية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The readings differ between a damma and kasra on qaf, both are Arabic forms; another group read the word with ṣād, and the intended sense is any accurately adjusted balance.
rows.anchor: واللفظة منه للمبالغة من القسط

rows.speaker: أبو حاتم
rows.claim: Abu Hatim says only the Kufans read qistas with kasra and advises against following a reading that has not spread to the two sanctuaries and Basra; Ibn Atiyya presents this as his statement.
rows.anchor: قال أبو حاتم إنما قرأ بكسر القاف أهل الكوفة

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Ibn Atiyya rejects Mujahid’s view that the scale at resurrection is only a metaphor for justice, affirming the Sunni belief in an actual scale with a shaft and two pans.
rows.anchor: وعقيدة أهل السنة أنه ميزان له عمود وكفتان

rows.speaker: أبو الفضل الجوهري
rows.claim: The preacher Abu al-Fadl al-Jawhari used the hand’s shape on a scale as a reminder: the fingers resemble the written forms of alif, lam, and ha, as if the balance says “Allah.”
rows.anchor: وسمعت أبي رضي الله عنه يقول رأيت الواعظ أبا الفضل الجوهري في جامع عمرو بن العاص

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatadah says taʾwīl here means the eventual outcome; Ibn Atiyya also allows the sense that good will result for people who measure and weigh fairly.
rows.anchor: «التأويل» في هذه الآية المآل. قاله قتادة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The aim in measuring and weighing is to seek accuracy; an unavoidable tiny shortfall made without intent is excused because perfect avoidance is beyond one’s capacity.
rows.anchor: والفرض من أمر الكيل والوزن تحري الحق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Qif means both to say and to follow; this begins his explanation of the prohibition on pursuing what one does not know.
rows.anchor: وقوله ولا تقف معناه ولا تقل ولا تتبع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Qafw is used for accusation and slander; a prophetic saying denies that Banu al-Nadr accuse their mother or disown their father.
rows.anchor: قول النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم: «نحن بنو النضر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas and Mujahid explain qif as “do not accuse”; Arabic usage also connects it to tracking an imprint or trace.
rows.anchor: وأصل هذه اللفظة من اتباع الأثر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse broadly forbids false speech, slander, and similar reprehensible claims made without knowledge.
rows.anchor: فهذه الآية بالجملة تنهى عن قول الزور والقذف وما أشبه ذلك من الأقوال الكاذبة الردية

rows.speaker: الكسائي
rows.claim: Al-Kisa'i reports a variant reading with qaf marked by damma and fāʾ quiescent.
rows.anchor: فيما حكى الكسائي «ولا تقف» بضم القاف وسكون الفاء

rows.speaker: الجراح
rows.claim: Al-Jarrah read fuʾād with an opened fāʾ; Abu Hatim and others rejected that dialectal form.
rows.anchor: «والفآد» بفتح الفاء وهي لغة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The senses are called “those” and treated as accountable because they perceive; Sibawayh gives the same rationale for describing the stars as prostrating.
rows.anchor: وجعلها في هذه الآية مسؤولة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The pronoun in “about it” may refer to what one does not know: God will ask the person’s hearing, sight, and heart about ungrounded claims, and the organs will expose him.
rows.anchor: والضمير في عنه يعود على ما ليس للإنسان به علم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alternatively, “about it” may refer to hearing, sight, and heart; the person will be asked about what those faculties perceived and their errors, with “their deeds” understood by ellipsis.
rows.anchor: ويحتمل أن يعود الضمير في عنه على كل التي هي للسمع والبصر والفؤاد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Marahan, read with a fatḥa, describes someone absorbed in worldly enjoyment and comfort; the verse forbids walking in that manner and reminds people that they cannot overpower the earth or equal the mountains.
rows.anchor: مصدر من مرح يمرح إذا تسبب مسرورا بدنياه مقبلا على راحته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Although addressed to the Prophet, the prohibition applies to everyone.
rows.anchor: وخوطب النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم بهذه الآية والمراد الناس كلهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Going hunting merely for recreation without need falls under the prohibition; occasional rest that renews a person for worship or learning does not.
rows.anchor: وإقبال الناس على الصيد ونحوه تنزها دون حاجة إلى ذلك داخل في هذه الآية

rows.speaker: يعقوب
rows.claim: A group, as reported by Ya'qub, read marahan with kasra as an active participle; al-Tabari’s interpretation then makes the verse address the proud person’s boastful arrogance at all times.
rows.anchor: «مرحا» بكسر الراء على بناء اسم الفاعل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: On the kasra reading, “you will not pierce the earth or reach the mountains” can mean that a proud person cannot break through or overtop them by boasting; this reading suits a constant trait of arrogance.
rows.anchor: وهو أن قوله لن تخرق الأرض ولن تبلغ الجبال طولا أراد به أنك أيها المرح المختال الفخور

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Kharq means traversing or cutting across the earth here, not making a hole in it; the author cites poetry for the word’s sense of broad terrain.
rows.anchor: والخرق الواسع من الأرض ومنه قول الشاعر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Readers differ between sayyiʾahu (possessive) and sayyiʾatan (indefinite); the first points back to all the preceding instructions, while the second singles out their bad elements as disliked by God.
rows.anchor: والإشارة على القراءة الأولى إلى ما تقدم ذكره مما نهي عنه كقول أف وقذف الناس والمرح وغير ذلك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: With the possessive reading, sayyiʾ is the subject of kāna and makrūhan its predicate; with sayyiʾatan, it is the predicate.
rows.anchor: فإعراب قراءته بين: وسيىء اسم كان ومكروها خبرها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Grammarians differ over makrūhan: one group makes it a second predicate agreeing with the sense of kull, while others treat it as an adjective of sayyiʾah.
rows.anchor: فقالت فرقة هو خبر ثان ل كان

rows.speaker: أبو علي الفارسي
rows.claim: Abu Ali al-Farisi rejects treating the masculine makrūhan as an adjective of the feminine noun and permits instead an apposition or a circumstantial accusative referring to the pronoun in “with your Lord.”
rows.anchor: وضعف أبو علي الفارسي هذا

rows.speaker: عبد الله بن مسعود
rows.claim: Ibn Mas'ud is reported to have read “its evils” as sayyiʾāt, with one report omitting the final hāʾ, and another using khabīthah.
rows.anchor: وقرأ عبد الله بن مسعود «كان سيئاته»

rows.speaker: الجراح
rows.claim: Al-Jarrah al-A'rabi read takhruq with a damma on rāʾ; Abu Hatim says he does not recognize this dialect.
rows.anchor: قرأ الجراح الأعرابي «تخرق» بضم الراء

rows.speaker: الطبري
rows.claim: Al-Tabari links these prohibitions back to “Your Lord decreed that you worship none but Him” (17:23); Ibn Atiyya says that connection is not clear.
rows.anchor: وذهب الطبري إلى أن هذه النواهي كلها معطوفة على قوله أولا:

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “That” refers to the preceding rules of conduct: they are wise, disciplined practices by which God cultivates virtuous character; the ban on another deity continues the earlier prohibitions.
rows.anchor: الإشارة ب ذلك إلى هذه الآداب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The address is to the Prophet but applies to every hearer; a madḥūr is humiliated and driven away.
rows.anchor: والخطاب للنبي عليه السلام، والمراد كل من سمع الآية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God challenges the Arabs’ claim that angels are His daughters: they claim sons for themselves but attribute daughters to God, a glaringly inconsistent and grave assertion.
rows.anchor: خطاب للعرب التي كانت تقول الملائكة بنات الله

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: A report from Qatadah, attributed to an unnamed scholar, says the verse addressed Jews who claimed angels were God’s daughters; Ibn Atiyya prefers the Arab context followed by most commentators.
rows.anchor: عن قتادة عن بعض أهل العلم أنه قال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Most readers pronounce ṣarrafnā with a doubled rāʾ, meaning that God varied rulings and admonitions in the Qur’an; al-Hasan’s lighter reading means that God directed people toward guidance through the call to Him.
rows.anchor: على معنى صرفنا فيه الحكم والمواعظ

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Hasan reads ṣarrafnā with a light rāʾ and understands it as God directing people toward guidance by calling them to Him.
rows.anchor: على معنى صرفنا فيه الناس إلى الهدى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some who doubled the rāʾ treat fī as extra and construe “varied in this Qur’an” as “varied this Qur’an”; Ibn Atiyya calls that weak.
rows.anchor: والتقدير ولقد صرفنا هذا القرآن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The majority read li-yadhakkarū; Hamza, al-Kisa'i, Talha, Yahya, and al-A'mash read the verb with a still consonant and a damma on kāf.
rows.anchor: «ليذكروا» بسكون الذال وضم الكاف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The expectation implied by the verse is from the human perspective; nufūr means intense turning away, likened to an animal’s flight.
rows.anchor: وما في ضمن الآية من ترج وطماعية فهو في حق البشر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn Atiyya cites a Gospel saying that Israel was called and lamented for but did not respond with longing or tears.
rows.anchor: يا بني إسرائيل شوقناكم فلم تشتاقوا ونحنا لكم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One interpretation says that if rival gods existed, they would seek nearness and favor with the Lord of the Throne, as in the Qur’anic use of “a path to your Lord.”
rows.anchor: فحكى الطبري وغيره من المفسرين أن معناه لطلب هؤلاء الآلهة الزلفى إلى ذي العرش والقربة إليه

rows.speaker: سعيد بن جبير
rows.claim: Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Abu Ali al-Farisi, al-Naqqash, and theologians interpret the rivals as seeking a way to challenge God’s sovereignty and power; this presents an argument from mutual prevention, linked to 21:22.
rows.anchor: وقال سعيد بن جبير وأبو علي الفارسي والنقاش وقاله المتكلمون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If two deities willed opposite outcomes for one body, both wills could not prevail and neither could fail without contradiction; whichever will failed would show its holder was not divine.
rows.anchor: إنا لو فرضناه لفرضنا أن يريد أحدهما تسكين جسم والآخر تحريكه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The claim that two gods always agree does not solve the problem: their disagreement is logically possible, and if two were admitted, three and then endlessly many would also be possible.
rows.anchor: اختلافهما جائز غير ممتنع عقلا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A further proof is that each indivisible element of created things can be brought into existence by only one power, so divine powers cannot be shared in producing it.
rows.anchor: إن الجزء الذي لا يتجزأ من المخترعات لا تتعلق به إلا قدرة واحدة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn Kathir and Hafs read “as they say” with yāʾ, while the majority address the hearers directly with tāʾ.
rows.anchor: «كما يقولون» بالياء من تحت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Subḥānahu is an unexpressed verbal noun meaning declaring God free of imperfection; taʿālā describes His greatness in rank, not a spatial or relational ascent.
rows.anchor: وسبحانه مصدر بفعل متروك إظهاره، فهو

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: On “what they say,” Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Asim, and Abu Amr read in the third person; Hamza and al-Kisa'i read in the second person.
rows.anchor: وقرأ حمزة والكسائي «تقولون» بالتاء من فوق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ʿUlūwwan is a verbal noun used in place of the verb, like the Qur’anic “God caused you to grow from the earth, a growth.”
rows.anchor: مصدر على غير الفعل، فهو كقوله والله أنبتكم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The heavens, earth, and their inhabitants declare God above the partners attributed to Him; “those in them” includes angels, humans, and jinn, and every thing praises and glorifies Him.
rows.anchor: المعنى ينزهه عن هذه المقالة التي لكم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The pronoun treating the heavens and earth as rational reflects that they perform the rational action of glorifying God.
rows.anchor: ثم أعاد على السماوات والأرض ضمير من يعقل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some scholars take universal glorification figuratively: created things reveal their Maker, and this sight prompts the reflective observer to glorify Him.
rows.anchor: فقالت فرقة هو تجوز

rows.speaker: عكرمة
rows.claim: Another group limits the general wording to living or growing things; Ikrima says a tree glorifies God, whereas a column does not.
rows.anchor: وقالت فرقة من شيء لفظ عموم، ومعناه الخصوص في كل حي ونام

rows.speaker: يزيد الرقاشي
rows.claim: Yazid al-Raqqashi says a dining tray once glorified God when it was a living, growing tree; after becoming a coated inanimate object, it did not.
rows.anchor: وقال يزيد الرقاشي للحسن وهما في طعام، وقد قدم الخوان: أيسبح هذا الخوان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A third group takes the wording literally and universally: every thing glorifies God in a manner humans neither hear nor comprehend; Ibn Atiyya answers that not understanding may describe heedless disbelievers who ignore the lesson in creation.
rows.anchor: وقالت فرقة: هذا التسبيح حقيقة

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Hasan reports that the Torah lists a thousand examples of creation glorifying God.
rows.anchor: وقال الحسن: بلغني أن معنى هذه الآية في التوراة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Readings vary between yusbbiḥu and tusabbiḥu, both of which Ibn Atiyya accepts; Ibn Mas'ud, Talha, and al-A'mash read “the heavens glorified.”
rows.anchor: والقراءتان حسنتان، وقرأ عبد الله بن مسعود وطلحة والأعمش «سبحت له السماوات»

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The closing names remind hearers that God patiently delays and pardons them despite their grave attribution, which every creature repudiates.
rows.anchor: إنه كان حليما غفورا فلذلك أمهلكم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The veil may be God’s protection of the Prophet from Meccan unbelievers who harmed him as he recited and prayed, or a barrier keeping unbelievers from understanding his recitation; the second reading links the verse to the next.
rows.anchor: هذه الآية تحتمل معنيين: أحدهما أن الله تعالى أخبر نبيه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Most naturally, mastūran qualifies the veil as hidden from people’s sight, a protection produced by divine power, care, and—on the alternative reading—misguidance.
rows.anchor: وقوله مستورا أظهر ما فيه أن يكون نعتا للحجاب

rows.speaker: الأخفش
rows.claim: Al-Akhfash says mastūr means sātir, as mashʾūm can mean shāʾim; Ibn Atiyya calls this needless strain and rejects the analogy.
rows.anchor: وقال الأخفش مستورا بمعنى ساتر كمشؤوم وميمون فإنهما بمعنى شائم ويأمن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The suggestion that mastūr is an intensive form like “poetic poet” is also challenged: such intensification should use an active participle from the same root.
rows.anchor: وقيل هو على جهة المبالغة كما قالوا شعر شاعر، وهذا معترض

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Akinna are coverings and waqr is heaviness in the ear that blocks hearing; these images depict the magnitude of the misguidance surrounding the unbelievers.
rows.anchor: الأكنة جمع كنان، وهو ما غطى الشيء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: When monotheism appears in recitation, Meccan unbelievers turn away because it repudiates their gods.
rows.anchor: يريد إذا جاءت مواضع التوحيد في القرآن أثناء قراءتك فر كفار مكة من سماع ذلك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some scholars recount that Quraysh came to visit Abu Talib, the Prophet recited monotheism and invited them to proclaim it, and they turned away; Ibn Atiyya says describing their reaction to his recitation best fits the wording.
rows.anchor: وقال بعض العلماء: إن ملأ قريش دخلوا على أبي طالب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Nufūran can be a circumstantial verbal noun or a plural meaning “fleeing ones”; the accusative then means they were fleeing.
rows.anchor: وقوله نفورا يصح أن يكون مصدرا في موضع الحال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An ya-fqahūhu is accusative with the sense “out of aversion to understanding it” or “to prevent them from understanding it”; the pronoun refers to the Qur’an.
rows.anchor: أن يفقهوه أن نصب على المفعول أي «كراهة أن»

rows.speaker: الطبري
rows.claim: Al-Tabari reports a view that the ones fleeing are the devils, although they are not named; the author compares it with the prophetic report that Satan retreats when the call to prayer is made.
rows.anchor: وحكى الطبري عن فرقة أنها قالت: إنما عنى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “What they listen with” refers to their manner of listening—mockery, disdain, and inattention—and the verse exposes their concealed attitude.
rows.anchor: والمراد بالذي ما ذكرناه من الاستخفاف والإعراض

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The words idh hum najw describe them with a collective verbal noun, like calling a people contentment or justice; another explanation takes it as their gathering in the Dār al-Nadwa.
rows.anchor: وقوله وإذ هم نجوى وصفهم بالمصدر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The more apparent meaning of masḥūran is a man whose mind and speech have been corrupted by sorcery, comparable to their charge that he is possessed.
rows.anchor: وقوله مسحورا الظاهر فيه أن يكون من السحر

rows.speaker: أبو عبيدة
rows.claim: Abu Ubayda instead derives masḥūr from saḥr, the lungs or bodily entrails, meaning a human who eats and drinks; the author says the following verse favors the sorcery sense because it frames their words as an analogy.
rows.anchor: أبو عبيدة: مسحورا معناه ذا سحر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The noun suḥūr is closer to saḥr (the bodily part) than siḥr (sorcery), though the two may be related just as ṣabūḥ derives from ṣabāḥ.
rows.anchor: ومنه السحور، وهو إلى هذه اللفظة أقرب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The next verse strengthens the derivation of masḥūr from sorcery: on Abu Ubayda’s bodily reading, the word is a literal description of a human rather than a figurative charge supported by their analogy.
rows.anchor: والآية التي بعد هذا تقوي أن اللفظة التي في الآية من السحر، بكسر السين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their labels for the Prophet—bewitched, sorcerer, madman, soothsayer—are comparisons rather than settled judgments; al-Walid ibn al-Mughira decided that sorcerer would most persuade visitors, and God declares them astray.
rows.anchor: ضرب المثل له هو قولهم مسحور، ساحر، مجنون، متكهن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “They cannot find a way” may mean no way to guidance and faith, as with the coverings over their hearts, or no way to ruin the Prophet’s mission by their accusations and schemes.
rows.anchor: وقوله فلا يستطيعون سبيلا يحتمل معنيين: أحدهما لا يستطيعون سبيلا إلى الهدى

rows.speaker: الطبري
rows.claim: Al-Tabari reports that the verse was revealed concerning al-Walid ibn al-Mughira and his companions.
rows.anchor: وحكى الطبري أن هذه الآية نزلت في الوليد بن المغيرة وأصحابه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse presents their denial, astonishment, and dismissal of resurrection; rufāt is matter worn down over time until it approaches dust, and the word follows a pattern for fragmented remains.
rows.anchor: من الأشياء: ما مر عليه الزمن حتى بلغ به غاية البلى

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas glosses rufāt as dust.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عباس: رفاتا غبارا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Even if they became stone, iron, or something still more formidable in their minds, the One who originated them the first time can restore them; their objection about who can restore them therefore fails.
rows.anchor: ثم احتج عليهم عز وجل في الإعادة بالفطرة الأولى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: They will shake their heads at the answer and ask when resurrection will occur; the answer “perhaps soon” affirms its nearness without fixing a date.
rows.anchor: يرفعون ويخفضون يريد على جهة التكذيب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: At the call, people rise from their graves by the blast in the Trumpet; responding means standing up and moving toward the summons.
rows.anchor: ويريد: يدعوكم من قبوركم بالنفخ في الصور

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas and Ibn Jurayj explain “with His praise” as “by His command”; Qatadah says it means in obedience and knowledge, but Ibn Atiyya says those explanations do not convey the wording.
rows.anchor: عن ابن عباس أنه قال معناه: بأمره

rows.speaker: ابن جبير
rows.claim: Ibn Jubayr’s explanation is that all creatures rise praising God for the power made manifest to them.
rows.anchor: كما قال ابن جبير، يقومون وهم يحمدون الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alternatively, “with His praise” can mean that the Prophet’s prediction will prove true, like saying “I was right, by God”; al-Tabari inclined this way but did not settle it.
rows.anchor: في هذه الآيات: عسى، أن الساعة قريبة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “You will think you remained only a little” may mean the resurrected lose awareness of worldly time, as sleepers do; al-Tabari supports this with 23:112–113.
rows.anchor: أحدهما أنه أخبر أنهم لما رجعوا إلى حالة الحياة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A second reading takes “think” as “know”: worldly life will be recognized as brief and finite, though Ibn Atiyya says this sense of certainty is awkward for an event already completed.
rows.anchor: والآخر: أن يكون الظن بمعنى اليقين

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatadah says that the horrors of Judgment will make people regard their worldly stay as very short.
rows.anchor: وحكى الطبري عن قتادة أنهم لما رأوا هول يوم القيامة احتقروا الدنيا

rows.speaker: سيبويه
rows.claim: Sibawayh treats “they say” as the response to an understood condition: if you tell My servants, they will speak in the best manner, since an imperative is not directly answered without an implied condition.
rows.anchor: فمذهب سيبويه، أنه جواب شرط مقدر

rows.speaker: الأخفش
rows.claim: Al-Akhfash allows the imperative itself to be answered and makes “they say” the response to “say.”
rows.anchor: ومذهب الأخفش: أن الأمر

rows.speaker: المبرد
rows.claim: Al-Mubarrad treats “they say” as the answer to an omitted imperative: “Tell My servants, ‘Say what is best,’ and they will say it.”
rows.anchor: أن يقولوا جواب لأمر محذوف

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjaj parses yaqulū as jussive after an understood li-, omitted because the preceding command makes the purpose clear.
rows.anchor: أن يقولوا جزم بالأمر، بتقدير قل لعبادي ليقولوا

rows.speaker: أبو عثمان المازني
rows.claim: Al-Mazini treats yaqulū as a fixed-form verb because it functions like the imperative “say”; Ibn Atiyya says the command means broad instruction to explain this practice, whose fruit is their best speech.
rows.anchor: أبي عثمان المازني في يقولوا أنه فعل مبني

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One group says “what is best” means the declaration that there is no god but God, but Ibn Atiyya finds the following warning about Satan’s discord poorly connected on that reading.
rows.anchor: فرقة: هي لا إله إلا الله

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: The majority understand the phrase as courteous, gracious conversation; al-Hasan gives examples such as “May God forgive you” and “May God have mercy on you.”
rows.anchor: وقال الجمهور: التي هي أحسن هي المحاورة الحسنى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The majority take “My servants” as the believers and differ over whether the command governs gracious manners among believers or gentle speech to Meccan polytheists during the truce; one report ties it to Umar’s near-violent reaction to an insult, with the verse later abrogated by the sword verse.
rows.anchor: وسبب الآية: أن عمر بن الخطاب رضي الله عنه شتمه بعض الكفرة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The opening of the following section reads yanziġ with a fatḥa on zāy; Talha read it with kasra, which Abu Hatim suspects may be dialectal. The word means Satan’s quick movement to cause harm.
rows.anchor: ومعنى النزغ: حركة الشيطان بسرعة ليوجب فسادا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The prophetic wording about Satan’s hand weapon explains nazgh as a sudden movement that may cause harm, rather than merely whispering.
rows.anchor: فهذا يخرج اللفظة عن الوسوسة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The preceding command best concerns believers’ manner toward Meccan unbelievers: they should not be harsh in religion, while God tells the unbelievers that He knows them and may guide them by repentance.
rows.anchor: هذه الآية تقوي أن التي قبلها هي ما بين العباد المؤمنين وكفار مكة

rows.speaker: ابن جريج
rows.claim: Ibn Jurayj and others gloss God’s mercy here as accepting their repentance from unbelief.
rows.anchor: يرحمكم بالتوبة عليكم من الكفر، قاله ابن جريج وغيره

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet’s duty is conveying the message, not acting as guardian over whether they believe.
rows.anchor: فإنما عليك البلاغ، ولست بوكيل على إيمانهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God’s knowledge and choice explain the different ranks of prophets; the passage answers Quraysh’s doubt that a human could be a messenger and points to Muhammad’s revelation and David’s Psalms.
rows.anchor: فهذه إشارة إلى محمد صلى الله عليه وسلم وإلى استبعاد قريش أن يكون الرسول بشرا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Prophetic superiority may be a general declaration that permits saying Muhammad is the best of humanity, or a distributed set of particular gifts among prophets; the Prophet forbade specifying superiority in the cases of Moses and Jonah.
rows.anchor: وتفضيل بعض الرسل، هو إما بهذا الإخبار المجمل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The majority read zabūran with fatḥa as a rare faʿūl form meaning “written”; Hamza, Yahya, and al-A'mash read it with damma, variously construed as a plural of Psalms or books, or as plural parts each called a zubūr.
rows.anchor: «زبورا» بفتح الزاي، وهو فعول بمعنى مفعول

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatadah says David’s Psalms contained admonitions, wisdom, and supplications, but no rules declaring lawful or unlawful.
rows.anchor: قال قتادة زبور داود مواعظ وحكم ودعاء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The bāʾ in “those in the heavens and earth” may be attached to an understood verb “He knows”; Ibn Atiyya says it can also attach directly to “knows best.”
rows.anchor: ويصح تعلقها ب أعلم ولا يلتفت لدليل الخطاب

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: The commanded interlocutors are not idol worshippers but worshippers of beings with reason; Ibn Abbas identifies them as worshippers of al-ʿUzayr, Christ, his mother, and the like.
rows.anchor: فقال ابن عباس: هي في عبدة العزيز والمسيح وأمه ونحوهم

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Another report from Ibn Abbas says the verses concern worshippers of the angels; he also includes worshippers of celestial bodies alongside al-ʿUzayr, Christ, and Mary.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عباس أيضا، وابن مسعود: هي في عبدة الملائكة

rows.speaker: ابن مسعود
rows.claim: Ibn Mas'ud also says the verses concern people who worshipped devils in the Prophet’s time; those devils later accepted Islam while their human worshippers continued worshipping them.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن مسعود أيضا: هي في عبدة شياطين كانوا في عهد رسول الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Whatever group is intended, the challenge is to invoke those beings in times of distress: they cannot remove or redirect the harm, and in reality they themselves seek nearness to God.
rows.anchor: فإنهم لا يملكون كشفه ولا تحويله عنكم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn Mas'ud and Qatadah read “you call upon” in the second person; the majority read “they call upon” in the third person, with the subject changing between the unbelievers and their deities.
rows.anchor: على قراءة ابن مسعود وقتادة «تدعون» بالتاء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Wasīlah means nearness and a means of reaching one’s objective; the deities worshipped by the unbelievers seek to draw near to their own Lord.
rows.anchor: والوسيلة، هي القربة، وسبب الوصول إلى البغية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God mentions Thamud to rebut anyone claiming that Quraysh would believe in a requested sign: Thamud received the she-camel yet wronged it, so they would not necessarily believe either.
rows.anchor: فذكر الله تعالى ثمود، بمعنى: لا تؤمنون إن تظلموا بالآية

rows.speaker: عنترة
rows.claim: Ibn Atiyya cites Antara’s line “men have a means of access to you” as evidence for the sense of wasīlah.
rows.anchor: إن الرجال لهم إليك وسيلة

rows.speaker: عمر بن الخطاب
rows.claim: Umar’s account of the Khaybar banner says people stayed up contending over who would receive it, illustrating the construction “which of them is nearer.”
rows.anchor: كما قال عمر بن الخطاب في حديث الراية بخيبر: فبات الناس يدوكون

rows.speaker: ابن فورك
rows.claim: Ibn Furak and others connect “those they call upon” to the prophets mentioned earlier, taking yadʿūna to mean that the prophets themselves pray to God; Ibn Atiyya also gives the ordinary reading as unbelievers invoking the deities, who seek nearness to God.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن فورك وغيره: إن الكلام من قوله أولئك الذين راجع إلى النبيين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Every town will perish before the Resurrection through ordinary death and extinction, or undergo a severe collective punishment; the phrase “from a town” indicates a class, though some restrict it to a wrong-doing town.
rows.anchor: أخبر الله تعالى في هذه الآية أنه ليس مدينة من المدن إلا هي هالكة

rows.speaker: النقاش
rows.claim: Al-Naqqash says he found in al-Dahhak’s commentary a survey predicting modes of destruction for known countries, including Andalusia’s ruin by horses and armies; Ibn Atiyya omits the other material for lack of reliability.
rows.anchor: وحكى النقاش أنه وجد في كتاب الضحاك بن مزاحم في تفسير هذه الآية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Towns may perish by drought, subsidence, flood, or civil strife; ruin by strife necessarily follows injustice, while drought and subsidence befall whomever God wills.
rows.anchor: فأما ما هلك بالفتنة، فعن ظلم ولا بد، إما في كفر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The town is destroyed through its inhabitants, and the passive reference to punishing it implies the people; the writing in the Book is the prior decree inscribed in the Preserved Tablet.
rows.anchor: وقوله في الكتاب يريد في سابق القضاء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrasing “nothing prevented Us” follows ordinary Arabic idiom: prior knowledge that earlier peoples would deny signs and be punished is called a prevention; the two an clauses have different grammatical cases.
rows.anchor: هذه العبارة في معناها هي على ظاهر ما تفهم العرب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Quraysh asked for the mountain of al-Safa to become gold and for mountains to be removed to make fields; God offered to grant the signs but warned that refusal would bring immediate punishment, and the Prophet chose respite.
rows.anchor: وسبب هذه الآية أن قريشا اقترحوا على رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjaj links the passage to the declaration that the Hour is the appointed time for this community’s unbelievers (54:46).
rows.anchor: قال الزجاج: أخبر تعالى أن موعد كفار هذه الأمة الساعة

rows.speaker: هارون
rows.claim: Harun says Kufans pronounce Thamud with nunation in every grammatical position; Abu Hatim says established Qur’an reciters do not, and notes the written alif is not pronounced.
rows.anchor: قال هارون: أهل الكوفة ينونون «ثمودا» في كل وجه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Mubṣirah is a relational form meaning that the she-camel came with sight, that is, it made its proof and miraculous nature plain; variants with a damma or fatḥa on mīm also mean manifest or perceptible.
rows.anchor: وقوله مبصرة على جهة النسب أي معها إبصار

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase “they wronged by it” means they put the act in the wrong place by hamstringing the she-camel; another view takes it as disbelief concerning the sign.
rows.anchor: وقوله فظلموا بها أي وضعوا الفعل غير موضعه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ordinary signs such as eclipses, thunder, earthquakes, and rainbows are warnings that allow time rather than bringing immediate punishment; al-Hasan also includes widespread death, as in the Ibn Mas'ud-era quake report.
rows.anchor: فمن ذلك الكسوف والرعد والزلزلة وقوس قزح

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Signs for reflection are of three kinds: universal signs available to learned observers, recurring natural events that alert the heedless, and miracles whose prophetic era has ended but which invite reflection on past revelation.
rows.anchor: وآيات الله المعتبر بها ثلاثة أقسام

rows.speaker: الطبري
rows.claim: Al-Tabari takes God’s encompassing the people to mean protecting and preserving Muhammad from the unbelievers; Ibn Atiyya calls this clear and fitting, though it connects less strongly with what follows. A similar report comes from al-Hasan and al-Suddi.
rows.anchor: أي في منعك يا محمد وحياطتك وحفظك، فالآية إخبار له

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Most commentators identify the vision as the Prophet’s waking vision on the Night Journey; Quraysh mocked the claim of a round trip to Jerusalem in one night, and some weak Muslims were led astray. On this reading, God’s encompassing means control over people’s guidance and misguidance, so Muhammad need not grieve over their disbelief.
rows.anchor: فقال الجمهور: هي رؤيا عين ويقظة

rows.speaker: النقاش
rows.claim: Al-Naqqash says the verse uses ruʾyā according to the assumption of those who considered the vision a dream, although in reality it was not.
rows.anchor: وقال النقاش جاء ذلك على اعتقاد من اعتقد أنها منامة وإن كانت الحقيقة غير ذلك

rows.speaker: عائشة
rows.claim: Aisha says the Night Journey vision was a dream; Ibn Atiyya says most commentators disagree and that the verse rules out her view because a dream would not be a trial or something people would reject.
rows.anchor: وقالت عائشة الرؤيا في الإسراء رؤيا منام

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas identifies the vision as the Prophet’s vision that he would enter Mecca; when he was turned back at al-Hudaybiya, some Muslims were tested by the delay.
rows.anchor: ابن عباس: الرؤيا التي في هذه الآية

rows.speaker: سهل بن سعد
rows.claim: Sahl ibn Sa'd reportedly identified the vision as the Umayyads leaping onto the Prophet’s pulpit; the report continues in the following segment.
rows.anchor: وقال سهل بن سعد: إنما هذه «الرؤيا» أن رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn Atiyya calls the Umayyad-vision view a weak, later invention and says it is not authentically attributed to Sahl ibn Sa'd; on that reading, the tree trial would concern Umayyad rulers, but the author favors the Night Journey interpretation and excludes Uthman, Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz, and Muawiya from the vision.
rows.anchor: وهذا قول ضعيف محدث، وليس هذا عن سهل بن سعد

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Al-Tabari transmits from Ibn Abbas that the cursed tree means the person who eats from it is cursed, since the tree had not been mentioned earlier; Ibn Atiyya says the Qur’anic wording can emphasize that curse.
rows.anchor: وقال الطبري عن ابن عباس: إن الشجرة الملعونة يريد الملعون آكلها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another group construes “cursed” as “banished and detested,” an apt description of a tree rooted in Hell and far from God’s mercy.
rows.anchor: وهذا أراد لأنها لعنها بلفظ اللعنة المتعارف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The warning may concern either Meccan unbelievers or later Umayyad rulers; Ibn Atiyya prefers the former as stated earlier.
rows.anchor: إما كفار مكة، وإما الملوك من بني أمية بعد الخلافة

rows.speaker: النقاش
rows.claim: Al-Naqqash says the increase in great transgression was revealed in connection with Abu Jahl’s mocking demonstration of eating dates with butter as “zaqqum.”
rows.anchor: فقد قال النقاش إن في ذلك نزلت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-A'mash read yukhawwifuhum; the majority read wa-nukhawwifuhum.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الأعمش «ويخوفهم» وقرأ الجمهور
